node.label: J. G. A. Pocock
node.date_label: The Ancient Constitution and the Feudal Law (1957) · The history of political thought: a methodological inquiry (1962) · The Machiavellian Moment (1975) · Concepts and Discourses: A Difference in Culture? (1996) · Barbarism and Religion: volumes 1 and 2 (1999) · Barbarism and Religion: volume 6, Barbarism: Triumph in the West (2015) · John Robertson, John Pocock’s Histories of Historiography (2025)
node.description: A historian of political thought and historiography who reconstructs the languages in which political thinking becomes possible. His methodological inquiry treats thinking as historical activity rather than only as coherent philosophy. The Machiavellian Moment presents a selective inquiry into republican fragility in time. In the 1996 concepts-and-discourses exchange he welcomes conceptual lexicons but questions whether they can reconstruct the complexity of political languages, and criticizes Skinner’s search for the modern state for risking anachronistic categories. John Robertson’s later account follows the historiographical problem from the ancient constitution to the six volumes of Barbarism and Religion; those books remain mediated rather than newly read here.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Ancient Constitution and the Feudal Law (1957, known through bibliography and John Robertson’s account); “The history of political thought: a methodological inquiry” (1962, selected 2009 reprint); The Machiavellian Moment (1975, introduction read in the retained source review); “Concepts and Discourses: A Difference in Culture?” (1996); Barbarism and Religion (six volumes, 1999–2015; dated and discussed through Robertson, 2025).
node.scope_note: Fresh reading 2026-10-24: printed pp. 3–4, 9–11 in the 2009 publisher excerpt of the 1962 methodological inquiry; the complete 1996 concepts-and-discourses contribution pp. 47–58; Robertson’s 2025 article pp. 1–4 closely, with later sections/endnotes consulted for the six-volume sequence. The earlier reading of The Machiavellian Moment introduction vii–x is preserved, not represented as a newly read complete book. No body of the 1957 or 1999–2015 books was read. Pocock explicitly cannot read German and discusses the Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe through Richter; the new objections preserve that limit and his praise of complementary inquiry. His private correspondence and late political essays were not read. The 1996 publication is separate from the December 1992 symposium.

proposed_edges.relationship: Treats political thinking as historical activity within available languages and distinguishes this inquiry from extracting only systematically coherent philosophy (1962; reformulated 1996).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Selected 1962 reprint pp. 3–4, 9–11 and 1996 pp. 47–50 read. This is an individual contribution within the contextual field, not an exclusive founding claim. The existing collective field-to-intellectual-history arrow, also naming Skinner and Brett, is preserved.

proposed_edges.relationship: Asks whether an alphabetical history of concepts can reconstruct the complexity of political languages and avoid projecting the historian’s categories onto earlier actors (published 1996).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Pocock, Concepts and Discourses, pp. 47–55, especially pp. 50–55. He explicitly cannot read German and responds to Richter’s presentation of the lexicon. He welcomes a complementary conceptual history and does not dismiss Koselleck’s project or claim first-hand inspection of all its articles. The distinction is an acknowledged methodological challenge, not an assertion that Cambridge and conceptual history are mutually exclusive schools.

proposed_edges.relationship: Singles out Skinner’s search for the modern concept of the state as exposed to the risk of imposing later categories on language users who did not employ those terms (published 1996).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Pocock pp. 54–55 and p. 55 n. 2 explicitly name The Foundations of Modern Political Thought, volume II’s conclusion (1978), and the essay The State. This specific criticism coexists with substantial sympathy for Skinner’s general methodological contention and intellectual collaboration. The cited books/essay were not newly read or independently judged here.

verification.note: Official institutional full PDF. Preface pp. 5–6, Richter pp. 7–9, Pocock pp. 47–58 and Koselleck pp. 59–66 read closely; final reply pp. 67–70 consulted for concluding context. Copyright/preface date the publication to 1996; the preface dates the symposium to December 1992. Claims are dated to the published text, not assumed identical to an uncollated oral delivery. Pocock explicitly says he does not read German and responds through Richter’s presentation. His criticism of the lexicon and his particular criticism of Skinner coexist with openness to complementary methods. Koselleck argues for interdependence, not an opposition between two homogeneous schools. Other contributions and original German lexicon entries unread, except as stated. No new direct quotations.

Printed pp. 1–4 read closely, later discussion and endnotes consulted for the six-volume Barbarism and Religion dates (1999–2015) and its first/last volume titles. Robertson’s account is explicitly a named reader’s reconstruction, not new reading of Pocock’s books. His criticism of Pocock’s late sovereign narratives remains a reader’s judgment; those essays and the cited private correspondence were not read and no new claim from them is proposed here. No claim that this 2025 article is Pocock’s own work.

edges_considered_not_proposed: Do not turn Pocock’s qualified lexical objection into refusal of all conceptual history.
No aggregate Cambridge-group edge is moved solely to Pocock.
